title: Detach from your work to make it work
author: itaydr
tldr: Designer Itay Dreyfus says caring too much about your own creative work stalls it. His fix is to treat personal projects with the distance you bring to client work, which is what finally lets him finish them.

keyPoints: Dreyfus spent about a month procrastinating over his own wedding invitation. Later, with his Niche design magazine issue about 90% done, he slowed to a crawl. He blames both on the same thing, deep personal attachment to the work.
He thinks the point of design is to finish and release work. Big goals like changing the world are, in his words, narcissistic aspirations that mostly live in job postings and pitch decks.

Meaningful work isn't supposed to be easy, he says, it's supposed to be progressable. He aims to move forward a little each day and to work without goals or metrics in mind, which shuts off the self-analysis and outcome prediction.

Projects tied to identity, like a designer's portfolio, attract endless revisions because every decision seems to say something about his whole practice. The same attachment that drives him also blocks him.

Client work came easier because he isn't the one making the final call. So he applied this 'client approach' to his own projects and pretended they belonged to someone else. That freed him to experiment, and he shipped the first issue.

He ends by asking readers to trust the process. Day to day, progress is slow and you can't see it. It only adds up to something real in retrospect, whether the work is writing, design, programming or music.
article.whyItMatters: Worth reading if you're a designer, writer or indie maker stuck near the end of a personal project. The original has the personal anecdotes, plus quotes from Trent Reznor, Are.na co-founder Charles Broskoski and Henrik Karlsson that make the advice concrete.
